newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN URGES ISRAEL TO CEASE TORTURE.
newsitem.headline: UN URGES ISRAEL TO CEASE TORTURE.

text.p: The U.N. Committee against Torture called on Israel on Friday to stop interrogating Palestinian detainees with methods including sleep deprivation and violent shaking, which the panel said constituted torture and broke international law.

The committee said the 1987 Convention against Torture, which Israel has signed, ruled out invoking the threat of terrorism as justification for cruel treatment, and told Israel to report back on steps taken by September 1.
But Israeli ambassador Yosef Lamdan rejected the committee's conclusions, saying they were based on the "hearsay evidence" of non-governmental organisations.

"It is absolutely not the case that Israel uses torture or any methods tantamount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in interrogating suspected terrorists," Lamdan said in a statement. "Israel has nothing to hide on this issue".

The U.N. committee listed seven interrogation methods which "appear to be applied systematically" and said Israel had neither confirmed nor denied reports of their use. "The committee therefore, must assume them to be accurate".

Practices reported by Amnesty International and other groups who have interviewed people interrogated by Israel's General Security Services, were: restraining people in very painful conditions; hooding; sounding of loud music for prolonged periods; sleep deprivation; threats including death threats to the victim and others; violent shaking; and using cold air to chill detainees.

Peter Burns, a Canadian professor who is the committee's rapporteur investigator on Israel, told Reuters: "Individually and in combination the methods constitute torture. Clearly they are cruel and degrading."

Bent Sorensen, a Danish doctor and vice-chairman of the committee, said the conclusions were also based on "medical evidence" contained in autopsy reports as well official Israeli court records showing length of sleep deprivation.

"Typical is 46 hours interrogation, two hours rest, then 36 hours interrogation, two hours rest," he said. "We have it all on paper -- not non-governmental organisations' papers but papers from the High Court of Israel."

Sorensen cited the example of a detainee who died in 1995 during interrogation. His autopsy was seen by professor Dale Pounder, a top forensic expert, who attributed death to brain damage caused by shaking, a controlled method of torture.
Burns said that the committee could not accept Israel's "defence of necessity" to justify cruel methods.

Nili Arad, director-general of Israel's Justice Ministry of Justice, told the committee on Wednesday that her country was in a constant struggle to strike a balance between protecting innocent civilians from terrorist violence while also respecting human rights.

Applying "moderate use of physical pressure" during some interrogations, allowed under Israel's Landau Commission rules, had helped investigators to foil 90 plans for large-scale terrorist attacks, she added.
The committee's 10 independent experts also expressed concern that a decision by the Israeli Supreme Court last November had the effect of sanctioning some of the interrogation practices.
"We also recommended that the terms of the Convention should be incorporated into the domestic law of Israel, particularly the definition of torture as contained in Article One," Burns said.
